title: Vast Emptiness, No Sage
author: Zhiyu
excerpt: Emperor Wu of Liang asked Great Master Bodhidharma: “What is the foremost meaning of the holy truth?” Bodhidharma said: “Vast emptiness, no sage!” The Emperor said: “Who, then, is facing me?” Bodhidharma said: “I don’t know.” The Emperor did not awaken, and Bodhidharma thereupon crossed the river to Wei.

inline.s: (This koan is excerpted from the Blue Cliff Record.)

Emperor Wu of Liang asked Great Master Bodhidharma: “What is the foremost meaning of the holy truth?” Bodhidharma said: “Vast emptiness, no sage!” The Emperor said: “Who, then, is facing me?” Bodhidharma said: “I don’t know.” The Emperor did not awaken, and Bodhidharma thereupon crossed the river to Wei.

Emperor Wu of Liang asked Great Master Bodhidharma: “What is the foremost meaning of the holy truth?” Bodhidharma said: “Perfectly still and empty—where is there any sage?” Emperor Wu then asked: “Then who is it that faces me?” Bodhidharma said: “I don’t know.” Emperor Wu failed to awaken, so Bodhidharma crossed the Yangtze River and went to the Northern Wei.
[Emperor Wu of Liang

] Xiao Yan, founder of the Liang dynasty of the Southern Dynasties. He once donned the kasaya and personally lectured on the Prajñā Sutra of Emitting Light. He devoted himself to the Way and served the Buddha, issuing imperial edicts throughout the land, building temples, ordaining monks, and practicing according to the teachings; people called him the “Son of Heaven with the Buddha-mind.” [The Northern and Southern Dynasties] From the year
when the Eastern Jin fell, to the year

when the Sui unified the realm—a span of one hundred seventy years—China formed a north–south standoff called the Northern and Southern Dynasties. The southern dynasties ran through Song, Qi, Liang, and Chen; the northern dynasties through the Northern Wei (later split into the Eastern Wei and Western Wei), the Northern Qi, the Northern Zhou, and others. [The holy truth] The truth perceived by sages. [The foremost meaning] The supreme, most profound subtle principle. [Vast emptiness] The appearance of empty stillness. [“I don’t know”] Not recognizing. Seen in light of the true aspect of all phenomena, originally there is not a single thing, so there is no question of knowing; hence the answer: “I don’t know.”
[The true aspect of all phenomena] The actual condition of all dharmas. The Buddha Pitaka Sutra says:
“What is called the true aspect of all phenomena? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything whatsoever.”

The True Aspect of All Phenomena

Later the Emperor raised this exchange with Master Zhigong. Zhigong asked: “Does Your Majesty know this man?” The Emperor said: “I don’t know.” Zhigong said: “This is the great Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, come to transmit the Buddha’s mind-seal.” The Emperor regretted it, and thereupon sent an envoy to invite him back. Zhigong said: “Never mind Your Majesty sending an envoy to fetch him—even if the whole
hé
, meaning “entire”)
nation went, he would not return.”

Later Emperor Wu brought this exchange to Master Bao Zhigong. Zhigong asked: “Does Your Majesty recognize this man (do you truly know who this man really is)?” Emperor Wu said: “I don’t know.” Zhigong said: “This is the great Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, come to transmit the Buddha’s mind-seal.” Emperor Wu deeply regretted it and wished to send an envoy to invite him back. Zhigong said: “Never mind Your Majesty sending an envoy to invite him back—even if every person in the entire nation went to ask, he would not return.”
[Bao Zhigong] Master Bao Zhi (

), also called Zhigong or the great sage Bao Zhi, was an eminent monk of the Qi and Liang periods of the Northern and Southern Dynasties. Born in Dongyang Town of Jurong County (now part of Qixia District, Nanjing), he was a native of Jincheng (present-day Lanzhou, Gansu), with the lay surname Zhu. Throughout his life he repeatedly displayed supernatural wonders.

[To transmit the Buddha’s mind-seal] Bodhidharma saw from afar that this land possessed the capacities of the Mahayana, and so came across the sea to transmit the Buddha’s mind-seal. [The mind-seal] “Mind” is the Buddha-mind; “seal” means the seal of approval, the seal of confirmation. The Chan school establishes no written words and relies on no speech, but only transmits mind to mind, using the Buddha-mind to seal and confirm the minds of beings, realizing the mark of non-duality.

[Non-duality] The principle of the one reality, so-of-itself and equal, without distinction between this and that, is called non-duality. A Bodhisattva’s awakening to the principle of the one reality and equality is called entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality.

In the above exchange, Emperor Wu viewed and questioned from the standpoint of the conventional truth, while Patriarch Bodhidharma viewed and answered from the standpoint of the ultimate truth—naturally they could not come to agreement. Bodhidharma had wished to deliver Emperor Wu, but the Emperor could not awaken; he was not a vessel of the true vehicle, so how could the Buddha’s mind-seal be transmitted to him? He had no choice but to leave him and go. Hence Zhigong said: “Never mind Your Majesty sending an envoy to invite him back—even if every person in the entire nation went to ask, he would not return.”

[The two truths] the conventional truth and the ultimate truth. The conventional truth is also called the worldly truth or the truth of worldly convention, namely the appearances of the world as perceived by ordinary people. The ultimate truth is also called the truth of the foremost meaning or the supreme truth, namely the true principle seen by sagely wisdom—the true aspect of all phenomena.
Vast emptiness, no sage:
Perfectly still and empty—where is there any sage?

This is said with reference to the true aspect of all phenomena, wherein the ordinary and the sage alike are extinguished. If there is not even a sage, how could there be any holy truth? (His intent was to lead Emperor Wu to awaken into the true aspect of all phenomena.)
Who, then, is facing me:

Who is it that faces me? Because Bodhidharma was a sage, Emperor Wu consulted him on the foremost meaning of the holy truth. Bodhidharma answered: “Perfectly still and empty, there is no sage!” So Emperor Wu then asked: “Then who is it that faces me? (Meaning: are you not a sage? How can you say there is none!)”
I don’t know:

Bodhidharma answered: “I don’t know. (Meaning: originally there is not a single thing—what is there that could face you? Again he sought to lead Emperor Wu to awaken into the true aspect of all phenomena.)”
The Emperor did not awaken, and Bodhidharma crossed the river to Wei:

Though Patriarch Bodhidharma twice sought to awaken him (with “vast emptiness, no sage” and “I don’t know”), Emperor Wu was unable to enter; he was truly not a vessel of the true vehicle, so the Buddha’s mind-seal could not be transmitted to him, and Bodhidharma had no choice but to leave. Crossing the river to Wei, he faced the wall at Shaolin for nine years before receiving the Second Patriarch.

[The true vehicle] The true teaching. “Vehicle” uses raft and ferry, cart and carriage as metaphors for the teaching by which one crosses the sea of birth and death and reaches the other shore of nirvāṇa.

[Capacity] The root of a plant can grow branches, trunk, and leaves, and a vessel can hold things, yet what grows and what is held differ in size and amount; likewise, practitioners of the Way differ in ability, high and low, and so are compared to roots and vessels. The Commentary on the Mahavairocana Sutra says:
“Contemplate living beings, measure their capacities, and only then give to them.”
Later, recalling this matter, Emperor Wu personally composed an inscription saying:
“Alas! Seen yet not seen, met yet not met, encountered yet not encountered—whether now or in antiquity, for such a loss one can only grieve and regret.”
And again he praised:
“When mind exists, for kalpas without end one lingers as an ordinary being; when mind is gone, in a single instant one ascends to wondrous enlightenment.”

[Kalpas without end] Kalpas of vast duration. [Whether now or in antiquity, one can only grieve and regret] Whether in the present or the past, whoever so misses such a golden opportunity will grieve and regret it without end.
Question: Emperor Wu built temples and ordained monks beyond number, so why did Patriarch Bodhidharma say he had no merit?
Answer: Emperor Wu gave with attachment to appearances, which is blessed virtue, not merit. Let us annotate this passage from the Compendium of the Five Lamps below to answer your question.

[Building temples] Constructing monasteries. [Ordaining monks] Helping people renounce home and become monks. [Blessed virtue] The blessings reaped from practicing the good deeds of humans and gods. Blessed virtue differs from merit: the outflow-tainted goodness of outwardly cultivated deeds is “blessed virtue,” while the inward realization of the outflow-free wisdom of the Buddha-nature is “merit.” Moreover, if one cultivates the Way while clinging to appearances, that is “blessed virtue”; if one leaves all appearances and cultivates all good, only then is it “merit.” [Outflows] “Outflow” is another name for affliction. Things that contain affliction are called “outflows.”

The Emperor asked: “Since I ascended the throne, I have built temples, copied sutras, and ordained monks beyond all counting. What merit is there?” The Patriarch said: “No merit at all.” The Emperor said: “Why is there no merit?” The Patriarch said: “These are but the small fruits of humans and gods, causes that carry outflows. Like a shadow following the form, though they exist they are not real.” The Emperor said: “What, then, is true merit?” The Patriarch said: “Pure wisdom, wondrous and perfect; its essence is of itself empty and still. Such merit is not to be sought through the world.”

Emperor Wu asked: “Since I (zhen) ascended the throne, I have built temples, copied sutras, and ordained monks beyond all counting. What merit is there?” Patriarch Bodhidharma said: “No merit at all.” Emperor Wu said: “Why is there no merit?” Bodhidharma said: “These are but the blessings of humans and gods, causes that carry outflows. Like a shadow following its form, though they have an appearance, they are not real.” Emperor Wu said: “What, then, is true merit?” Bodhidharma said: “Pure wisdom, wondrous and perfect; its essence is of itself empty and still—this alone is merit. Such merit cannot be sought through worldly dharmas.”

[Copying sutras] Transcribing Buddhist sutras. At that time there was no printing, so sutras were circulated by hand-copying. [Beyond all counting] Unable to be recorded one by one; an expression of extreme number. [Though they exist they are not real] The Song of Enlightenment says:

“Giving while clinging to appearances brings the blessings of heaven, like shooting an arrow up into empty space. When its force is spent the arrow falls back, drawing a future life of misfortune. How can this compare to the gate of the unconditioned true aspect, by which one leaps straight into the realm of the Tathagata?”
(For annotation see
Commentary on the Song of Enlightenment
) [Pure wisdom] Pure and clear wisdom. With this wisdom, illumining that all dharmas are empty, one attains inner stillness (the essence of itself empty and still).
